messages.subject: Longitudinal Growth Study - Computation Time Lengthy...
parts:
Hi Stan Users,

I'm thinking of using STAN, with 'rstan' package instead of using 'lme4' for a longitudinal 'growth' study design, because eventually I would like to include missing information for the 'X2' variable below and STAN is less computational demanding than JAGS or BUGS. The computation time for the model seems little slow. I've started with simple models and built up. The more partial pooling variables I add, the much more computationally demanding the model becomes. I am assuming slopes are fixed in the linear regression,but I may code a model where slopes are variable among individuals, increasing the computation time further.

I wonder if there is a more efficient way of coding this example or if I am coding the model incorrectly? That being said, I have approximately 3000 individuals, so I think the slow computation time may be just the number of parameters that STAN needs to estimate.

Following Gelman and Hill 2006 the multilevel model is:


Y[i,j] ~ Normal(alpha[k[i,j] + Beta1[X1[i,j] + Beta2[X2[i,j] +Beta3(X1[i,j]*X2[i,j,), sigma^2), for i = 1,...,n subjects, for j = 1 to 2,m gender.

The 'lmer' function in 'lme4' package would code the above as:

Model1 <- lmer(Y ~ X1 + X2 + X1:X2 + (1 | subject) + (1 | gender) 

The Stan code I am using is:

data {
  int<lower=0> N; //no. of observations
  int<lower=0> n_subject; //no. of subjects
  int<lower=0> n_gender; //no. of genders
  int<lower=1, upper=n_subject> subject[N]; // label for each subject or individual
  int<lower=1, upper=n_sex> gender[N]; // grouping gender
  vector[N] u1; //fixed or predictator variable
  vector[N] u2; //fixed or predicator variable 2 
  vector[N] y; //Y 'growth' variable
}
parameters {
  real b1;
  real b2;
  real b3;
  vector[n_subject] a1;
  vector[n_gender] a2;
  real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma_a1;
  real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma_a2;
  real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma_y;
}
transformed parameters{
  vector[N] y_hat;
  vector[N] inter; interaction term
  
  for (i in 1:N)
    inter <- u1*u2
    y_hat[i] <- b1*u1[i] + b2*u2[i] + b3*inter[i] + a1[subject[i]] + a2[gender[i]];
}  
model {
b1 ~ normal(0, 100);
b2 ~ normal(0, 100);
b3 ~ normal(0, 100);    
a1 ~ normal(0, sigma_a1);
a2 ~ normal(0, sigma_a2);
growth ~ normal(y_hat, sigma_y);
}

Cheers,

Allan

parts:
Don’t do real<lower=0, upper=100>.  Simply real<lower=0> is better.
Then add a prior for these parameters if you want.
Also, don’t do normal(0,100); better to do normal(0,10) or even normal(0,1).  I’m assuming your predictors have ben scaled reasonably.
A

>
> for (i in 1:N)
> inter <- u1*u2
> y_hat[i] <- b1*u1[i] + b2*u2[i] + b3*inter[i] + a1[subject[i]] + a2[gender[i]];

Can you send something that compiles?

u1 and u2 are both vectors, so you can't multiply
them like this. And you're missing semicolons and
brackets on the loop.

I'm not trying to be picky, I just don't know what
you intend with this.

The goal is to pull shared computations out and use
as much vectorization as you can, such as

y_hat <- b1 * u1 + b2 * u2 + b3 * inter;
for (n in 1:N)
y_hat[n] <- y_hat[n] + a1[subject[n]] + a2[gender[n]];

You might be able to go even further and compute the
n_subject x n_gender table of sums and double-index it
with a1_plus_a2[subject[n], gender[n]], but that's a pretty
extreme optimization and you probably shouldn't start there.

You can also define y_hat as a local variable in the model.
Unless you want to use it for inference later.

- Bob

Allan,

I'm pretty new to Stan too. I was recently very surprised (and ultimately pleased) at how much of a speed-up I got from using non-centered parameterization. I had a multilevel modeel too, but maybe a bit more deeply nested. So YMMV.

By non-centered, I mean try something like

transformed parameters {
  b1 <- b1_mu + b1_raw * b1_sd;
}

parameters { 
  real b1_mu;
  real<lower=0> b1_sd;
  real b1_raw;
}

model { 
  b1_raw ~ normal(0, 1); // implies b1 ~ normal(b1_mu, b1_sd)
}
​

Then you just use b1 in your model as you normally would. Also, you can just drop the b1_mu if you want to use a mean of 0.

​
Such a procedure was a truly massive speed-up for me. It was shocking! Good luck.

-Ryan

It turns out that the slowdown in computation was caused by the mislabeled data. I was using for "n_subject" was not numbered correctly, so instead of having  i = 1,...,10 subjects I had 8 subjects, with the label for subjects 7 and 8 missing. 

I tried the centering method you suggested, but YMMV. The computation time was worse with centering. However see below, I changed the entire modeling structure, I did some more reading on longitudinal modeling and I needed a multilevel linear model.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Longitudinal Growth Study - Computation Time Lengthy...
parts:
Hi everyone,

I finally had time to revisit the Longitudinal Growth Study using Stan. With some discussions, I ended up using a random-intercept for the random effect of individual in the study, instead of a random slope, random intercept and covariance structures. We were interested in the effect of gender/sex in the study, as well as the interactions between age and two covariates, we choose to include it as a factor. For our study, the R-code in 'lme4' package would be:
Model1 <-lmer(Y~F.sex+Age*C1*C2+(1|subject)

For STAN, the code would be:

data {
  int N; //number of data points
  real Y[N]; //growth
  real age[N]; //age
  real Fsex2[N]; //factor of gender coded as 1 for being sex "2" and 0 for not being sex "2"
  real C1[N]; //covariate 1
  real C2[N]; //covariate 2
  int subject_index[N];   //subject id
  int N_subject_index;
}
transformed data{
 real age_C1[N];  
 real age_C2[N]; 
 real C1_C2[N];    
 real age_C1_C2[N];
 for(i in 1:N){
 age_C1[i] <- age[i]*C1[i];
 age_C2[i] <- age[i]*C2[i];
 C1_C2[i] <- C1[i]*C2[i];
 age_C1_C2[i] <- age[i]*C1[i]*C2[i];
 }
}
parameters {
  real Intercept;   // Grand intercept
  real beta_age;    // could use a vector of betas instead, i.e. vector[9] Beta, but its easier to pick out each coefficient this way.
  real beta_Fsex2; 
  real beta_C1;
  real beta_C2;
  real beta_ageC1; // age_chum interaction
  real beta_ageC2; // age_npgo interaction
  real beta_C1C2;
  real beta_ageC1C2;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real vary_subject_index[N_subject_index];
  real<lower=0> sigma_subject_index;
} 
model {
  real vary[N];
  real glm[N];
    
  //priors
  Intercept ~ normal(0,10);  
  beta_age ~ normal(0,10);
  beta_Fsex2 ~ normal(0,10);
  beta_C1 ~ normal(0,10);
  beta_C2 ~ normal(0,10);
  beta_ageC1 ~ normal(0,10);
  beta_ageC2 ~ normal(0,10);
  beta_C1C2 ~ normal(0,10);
  beta_ageC1C2 ~ normal(0,10);
  sigma_subject_index ~ lognormal(0,1);  
  sigma ~ lognormal(0,1); 
    
  // Varying or Random effects   
  for ( j in 1:N_subject_index ) 
    vary_subject_index[j] ~ normal( 0 , sigma_subject_index );  
  
  // Fixed effects   
  for ( i in 1:N ) {      
    vary[i] <- vary_subject_index[subject_index[i]];      
    glm[i] <- vary[i] + Intercept 
    + beta_age * age[i] 
    + beta_Fsex2 * Fsex2[i]           
    + beta_C1*C1[i]
    + beta_C2*C2[i]
    + beta_ageC1*age_C1[i]
    + beta_agec2*age_C2[i] 
    + beta_C1C2*C1_C2[i]
    + beta_ageC1C2*age_C1_C2[i];   
  }  
  Y ~ normal(glm, sigma);
}
generated quantities{
  real vary[N];
  real glm[N];
  vector [N] log_lik;
  real dev;
  dev <- 0;
  for ( i in 1:N ) {  
    vary[i] <- vary_subject_index[subject_index[i]];      
    glm[i] <- vary[i] + Intercept 
     vary[i] <- vary_subject_index[subject_index[i]];      
    glm[i] <- vary[i] + Intercept 
    + beta_age * age[i] 
    + beta_Fsex2 * Fsex2[i]           
    + beta_C1*C1[i]
    + beta_C2*C2[i]
    + beta_ageC1*age_C1[i]
    + beta_agec2*age_C2[i] 
    + beta_C1C2*C1_C2[i]
    + beta_ageC1C2*age_C1_C2[i]; 
    log_lik[i] <- normal_log( growth[i] , glm[i] , sigma );
    dev <- dev + (-2)* normal_log(growth[i] , glm[i] , sigma);
  }
}

I ran 500 iterations and used 3 chains, I got covergence with this smaller amount iterations. messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Longitudinal Growth Study - Computation Time Lengthy...
parts:
You can make all that a bit faster.

If you convert your data types from arrays to vectors, you
can replace this

for(i in 1:N) {
age_C1[i] <- age[i]*C1[i];

with

age_C1 <- age .* C1;

This is more to prevent errors (e.g., bounds checks built in,
no indexes to fiddle) than for efficiency.


The big win will be expressing the linear predictor as
a vectorized operation. First, glm and everything else needs
to be defined as a vector rather than array. Then you can
replace

for ( i in 1:N ) {
vary[i] <- vary_subject_index[subject_index[i]];
glm[i] <- vary[i] + Intercept
+ beta_age * age[i]
+ beta_Fsex2 * Fsex2[i]
+ beta_C1*C1[i]
+ beta_C2*C2[i]
+ beta_ageC1*age_C1[i]
+ beta_agec2*age_C2[i]
+ beta_C1C2*C1_C2[i]
+ beta_ageC1C2*age_C1_C2[i];
}

with

glm <- Intercept
+ vary_subject_index[subject_index]
+ beta_age * age
+ beta_Fsex2 * Fsex2
+ beta_C1 * C1
+ beta_C2 * C2
+ beta_ageC1 * age_C1
+ beta_agec2 *age_C2
+ beta_C1C2 * C1_C2
+ beta_ageC1C2 * age_C1_C2;

You could even just put this all right inside normal, but defining
the variable and assigning isn't that expensive (cheap copy).

That still has a bunch of multiply-by-zero you don't need in
the Fsex2 case, which is a boolean indicator, but there's not
a great way to speed that up without writing a function that either
inserts aconstant 0 if Fsex2[n] is 0 and inserts beta_Fsex2 otherwise.
No useless multiplications by 1 or 0 that way.

vector fill_if(int[] include, real beta) {
vector[num_elements(vector)] v;
real z;
z <- 0;
for (i in 1:num_elements(vector))
if (include[i])
v[i] <- beta;
else
v[i] <- z;
}
}

and then replace

+ beta_Fsex2 * Fsex2

with

+ fill_if(Fsex2, beta_Fsex2)

It's goofy to define the zero and reuse it, but it's a bit more
efficient with memory than using v[i] <- 0, which creates a new
autodiff variable for each instance.

Finally, you want to use a non-centered parameterization and
replace this:

for ( j in 1:N_subject_index )
vary_subject_index[j] ~ normal( 0 , sigma_subject_index );

by making vary_subject_index a vector and using

vary_subject_index_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

and then replacing the line above

+ vary_subject_index[subject_index]

with

+ sigma_subject_index * var_subject_index_raw[subject_index]

- Bob
